items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.why: The four safeguards: information, representations, human intervention, contest. Applies only to significant decisions based solely on automated processing. Inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80; fully in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82).
items.quote: enable the data subject to contest such decisions

items.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 103: Complaints by data subjects
items.locator: s.103(2), inserting Data Protection Act 2018 s.164A(2)-(5); commencement note I2
items.why: Source of the figure (30 days to acknowledge, s.164A(3)). Controllers must facilitate complaints, respond without undue delay and inform the complainant of the outcome. In force 19 June 2026.
items.quote: the controller must acknowledge receipt of the complaint within the period of 30 days beginning when the complaint is received

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 82: Right to compensation and liability
items.why: Compensation for material or non-material damage from an infringement; a controller escapes only by proving it is not in any way responsible.
items.quote: shall have the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor for the damage suffered

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 124: Remedies: general
items.locator: s.124(2)-(7); see also s.119(4) for county court awards including injured feelings
items.why: Employment tribunal may declare, award compensation and recommend steps to reduce the adverse effect on the complainant. For unintentional indirect discrimination it must consider the other remedies before compensation (s.124(4)-(5)).
items.quote: order the respondent to pay compensation to the complainant; (c) make an appropriate recommendation

items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (white paper)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 3.2.3, box 'Principle: Contestability and redress' (after para 52)
items.why: Source of the quotation. The principle is non-statutory and addressed to regulators; it creates no new right for individuals.
items.quote: The UK's initial non-statutory approach will not create new rights or new routes to redress at this stage.

items.title: OECD AI Principles, 1.3: Transparency and explainability
items.why: The international baseline: information that enables those adversely affected to challenge an AI system's output. The challenge wording sits here, not in the accountability principle (1.5). Year of the 2024 update taken from oecd.ai; to confirm against the legal instrument.
items.quote: to provide information that enable those adversely affected by an AI system to challenge its output

items.title: FCA Handbook, DISP 1.3: Complaints handling rules
items.quote: undertake proactively a redress or remediation exercise, which may include contacting customers who have not complained
items.why: The sector rule the first pass left unchecked. A regulated firm must identify and remedy recurring or systemic problems, including root causes that affect products nobody has complained about (a rule), and should consider whether to seek out and compensate customers who have not complained (guidance). The closest thing in UK rules to the three steps this criterion describes. Applies to FCA-regulated firms only; 1.3.6 is guidance, tied to Principle 6.

items.title: FG22/5: Final non-Handbook Guidance for firms on the Consumer Duty
items.quote: If a firm identifies that it has caused customers harm, either through its action or inaction, the firm must act in good faith
items.why: States the duty in the regulator's own words: a firm that finds it has caused harm must act to put it right, consider redress, and pay it promptly when due. It applies whatever caused the harm, so it covers an unfair model as much as an unfair term. Guidance on the Consumer Duty for FCA-regulated firms dealing with retail customers; not a general duty on all businesses.

items.title: How to deal with data protection complaints
items.locator: Opening summary and 'Latest updates' (published 12 February 2026, updated 8 May 2026)
items.quote: You must have a process for handling data protection complaints within your organisation - there are no exemptions to this.
items.why: The regulator's guidance on the complaints duty the brief cites, which the first pass could not locate. Confirms the four steps: give people a way to complain, acknowledge within 30 days, respond without undue delay and tell them the outcome. About data protection complaints in general; it does not mention AI.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 16: Right to rectification
items.quote: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning him or her.
items.why: The individual's lever for the first step, correction: where an unfair outcome came from wrong data about the person, they can require it to be put right without undue delay. It corrects the record, not the decision made on it, and says nothing on other people affected by the same fault. Read in the first pass and left out for space.

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 119: Remedies
items.quote: An award of damages may include compensation for injured feelings (whether or not it includes compensation on any other basis).
items.why: The remedy for discrimination in services (lending, insurance, retail), where the claim goes to the county court or sheriff rather than an employment tribunal. The court may grant any remedy the High Court could, and damages can cover injured feelings. Unlike section 124 it gives no power to recommend steps. Corrects a gap the first pass recorded: the brief's 'tribunal' sentence covers employment only.

items.title: Principles for remedy
items.quote: returning the complainant and, where appropriate, others who have suffered similar injustice or hardship, to the position they would have been in
items.why: The UK public-sector standard for redress, and the source for extending a remedy beyond the person who complained to others harmed by the same fault. Also asks bodies to consider every form of remedy, including apology and explanation, and to learn from the outcome. Binding on no one; it states what the Ombudsman expects of government departments and the NHS. Dated February 2009 on its face; the Ombudsman's page shows it as last updated 30 September 2026.

items.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry Report: Volume 1 (human impact and redress)
items.publisher: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry (Sir Wyn Williams)
items.locator: Para 3.1, PDF p.12; Recommendation 2, section 2; section 6 on 'full and fair' redress and delay
items.quote: there are currently about 10,000 eligible claimants in the schemes providing financial redress
items.why: The UK's fullest official account of redress after people were wronged on the strength of a computer system's output. Finds that the number affected is almost impossible to establish, records four separate redress schemes, and recommends that government define 'full and fair' redress publicly. Shows the cost of the missing middle step, working out who was affected. Horizon was accounting software, not AI, and the wrongs were prosecutions and debts, not biased scoring.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 86: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure
items.why: Sits in the Act's section headed 'Remedies'. A person significantly affected by a decision based on a listed high-risk system can require the organisation using it to explain the system's role and the main elements of the decision. A right to an explanation, which makes a challenge possible; it is not a right to compensation or to a fresh decision. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal. EU law: reaches UK firms only where a system or its output is used in the EU. No application date is stated here.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 20: Corrective actions and duty of information
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: shall immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring that system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it
items.why: The 'fix the system' step as a legal duty: a provider that has reason to think its high-risk system does not conform must correct, withdraw, disable or recall it at once and tell distributors and the organisations using it. It is silent on the people already affected by the system's decisions, which is the gap this criterion tests. A duty on providers. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal. EU law: reaches UK firms only where a system or its output is used in the EU. No application date is stated here.

items.title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
items.locator: Para 29 (fairness and non-discrimination); para 35 (attributing responsibility in cases of remedy)
items.quote: Effective remedy should be available against discrimination and biased algorithmic determination.
items.why: International comparator. The plainest international statement that a person harmed by a biased algorithmic decision should have an effective remedy, and that responsibility in cases of remedy must always be traceable to a person or legal entity. Adopted by UNESCO's General Conference on 23 November 2021; a recommendation to states, not binding on companies.

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling (draft guidance): What are the ADM safeguards?
items.locator: Sections 'What is 'human intervention'?' and 'How do we enable people to contest decisions?'
items.quote: you must put measures in place for people to challenge or appeal the ADM you carry out
items.why: How the regulator reads the safeguards the brief lists: people must be told they can contest and how, and the person who reconsiders must be able to alter the decision, be trained, and look at the data it rested on; a token second look does not count. Covers significant decisions taken solely by automated means. Draft guidance, updated 31 March 2026; consultation closed, final text may differ.

items.title: Conceptualising Contestability: Perspectives on Contesting Algorithmic Decisions
items.publisher: Henrietta Lyons, Eduardo Velloso and Tim Miller (authors' copy on arXiv 2103.01774; published version DOI 10.1145/3449180)
items.quote: the ability to contest algorithmic decisions is being recognised as an important safeguard for individuals
items.why: Analyses what people and organisations said contestability should mean, from submissions on Australia's proposed AI ethics framework. Finds the idea disputed but understood as protection for the individual, modelled on how human decisions are challenged. Useful for designing the 'review affected decisions' step. Qualitative analysis of consultation responses in Australia; no evidence on outcomes.

items.title: Contestable AI by Design: Towards a Framework
items.publisher: Kars Alfrink, Ianus Keller, Gerd Kortuem and Neelke Doorn, Minds and Machines 33
items.quote: ensuring AI systems are contestable by design: responsive to human intervention throughout the system lifecycle
items.why: A peer-reviewed synthesis of the literature on building challenge and correction into a system from the start, rather than adding an appeals route afterwards. Supports the 'recurrence tracked' level: a fault found through one challenge should reach the people who maintain the system. A framework drawn from published papers, not tested in organisations; open access.
